title: Rights, consignment and artists selling their own albums
summary: How the festival recordings' rights are given up, flat fees, and artists selling albums themselves.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Yeah. Is it partsof the contract that you made when you appeared there? That's, you relinquished all rights to what you record.

Yes. Of course, today with the industry like it is, these things would probably never get any further than the box. It makes the producer and the performer pretty independent of each other, and at the same time, it's an opportunity for the performer to, let' say, benefit by performing; because he can always ger some of these albums on consignment, more or less. And then you're own your own if you have a way to dispose of them. Because one of the problems with the recording industry so far as we're concerned, is a matter of distribution.
Sure.
So a lot of the artists secure a certain amount of albums -- In fact, when the albums come out, the

producers usually supply the artist with a supply of recordings so that they can make some extra money, you know.
Yeah.
And, of course, after that, if you want to order some more albums, you can order them and --
Right now, a lot of artists are selling their albums right on the spot.
Sure.
At concerts or whatever.
Yeah.
And this is not a bad arrangement.
But very often though, it's the artists themselves who have produced the album.
Sure, a lot of times. Well, right now, it's the only way. I mean, if you have enough money to provide the overhead for making a recording during a session, you can go in business for yourself.
But this requires a pretty substantial

nest egg, because the record still has to pressed. And I don't know whether the manufacturer who presses albums -- whether he's willing to press just a small amount.
So you would have to order -- you'd have to supply yourself with thousands of albums. And, of course, that means that you got to sell a thousand albums.
But that's the way it's being done now.

This may be a naive question, but just let me ask it anyway. Is the making of records a way of financing a jazz festival, or is the jazz -- holding the jazz festival a way of bankrolling the making of records?
I don't think anyway you look at it, it's a paying proposition. The concert does not take care of itself.
When you bring forty and fifty musicians and you have to pay them, you do get paid for the performance plus your transportaion and accommodations -- hotel accommodations.
So that's a pretty big outlay there. And

then, of course, to edit and get out this album. The producer -- you know, he has to lay out a certain amount of funds to have available. So he's speculating with the hopes of something happening. It's very difficult for me to believe that there's a lot of money being made on the part of the producer. So far as I can see, in this particular case, the artist has the best advantage, because you perform. That's all you do, you get paid for the performance.
You get a flat fee.

You get a flat fee and you can peddle your own album if you're so inclined. I mean, you can make a lot of money. I mean, I know some musicians right now are selling their albums on the spot. And if you happened to have a steady job, you can get rid of a lot of albums that way. So, this is not the worst arrangement.
Yeah. How would you obtain

You get in touch with him and get them on consignment. He will charge you a rate and --
Could you give us some idea of what that might be?
Different ones have different charges. He will sell the album through the artist at the same rate that he would sell them to a distributor or a record shop.
Yeah.
And you can get them on consignment, you know. You can say 'send me a hundred albums.' As you sell them, you will pay him. Sometimes they run three dollars or three-fifty, say, something like that.
You generally sell them for double that amount.
Yes.

A lot of the artists today are advertising that they have albums available, then you can order them directly.
Of course, that entails another expense for which you would have to charge more for the album, because the handling and shipping charges are not cheap, you know.
And, of course, you have to include the tax and everything on your album. And so therefore, you have to take those under consideration.
I think for the most part, the musicians are taking their albums around with them.
Okay.
